domains.title: Application Security
domains.short_overview: Protecting a system's data, identity, and actions from unauthorized access or use.

children.title: Authentication vs Authorization
children.short_overview: Authentication proves who you are; authorization decides what an already-authenticated identity may do — a distinction frequently conflated, per the JWT/OAuth deep topic's own failure scenario.

sections.what: Authentication proves who you are; authorization decides what an already-authenticated identity may do — a distinction frequently conflated, per the JWT/OAuth deep topic's own failure scenario.
sections.how: This project's own risk_policy.py applies the authorization half of this distinction to AI actions (what may this agent auto-execute) rather than human identities.

children.title: Authentication & Authorization: JWT, OAuth2/OIDC & Spring Security
children.short_overview: The distinction between proving who you are and deciding what you're allowed to do, and the standard protocols/tokens that implement each at scale.

sections.why: Authentication and authorization are foundational to essentially every real backend system with more than one user, and are consistently tested in backend interviews both as concrete protocol knowledge (JWT structure, OAuth2 flows) and as a System Design topic (how to secure service-to-service calls). This project's own Customer app has explicitly not yet implemented an auth layer, making this honestly STUDY_SCENARIO/general knowledge rather than demonstrated project experience.
sections.history_evolution: HTTP Basic Auth (part of the original HTTP spec, 1990s) and server-side sessions (a session ID cookie referencing server-stored state) were the original web auth mechanisms — sessions require server-side state, which becomes awkward once an API must scale horizontally across many stateless servers or be consumed by non-browser clients (mobile apps, other services). OAuth 2.0 (finalized as RFC 6749, 2012, led by the IETF working group with heavy industry input from Google, Twitter, Facebook) standardized delegated authorization (letting an app act on a user's behalf without ever seeing their password) originally for third-party API access. JWT (JSON Web Token, RFC 7519, 2015) provided a compact, self-contained, cryptographically signed token format that let a server verify a token's authenticity without a database lookup — a natural fit for OAuth2's access tokens and for stateless API authentication generally. OpenID Connect (OIDC, 2014) layered a standardized *authentication* protocol (proving identity) on top of OAuth2's *authorization* framework, since OAuth2 itself was never actually designed to answer 'who is this user,' only 'what can this token do' — a frequently confused distinction even among practitioners.
sections.why_now: Authentication/authorization is needed the moment a system has more than one type of user or must restrict any action to specific identities — essentially every real product. JWTs specifically are justified when statelessness (no server-side session lookup needed to validate a request) and cross-service verification (any service holding the signing key/public key can verify a token independently) are valuable, such as in a microservices architecture; a simple server-side session is often simpler and sufficient for a single monolithic application with no cross-service verification need.
sections.big_picture: Business requirement: only the right identity can perform a given action, and that identity's authenticity can be verified cheaply and reliably on every request. NFR: authentication/authorization must not become a latency or availability bottleneck (a JWT's self-contained verification specifically avoids a database round trip on every single request, unlike a naive session-lookup design). Architecture: authentication (login, token issuance) typically happens once at a dedicated identity provider/auth server; authorization (checking a token's claims/scopes against what's needed for a specific action) happens on every subsequent request, ideally cheaply, at each service boundary.
sections.design_intellect: The core idea of a JWT is a self-contained, tamper-evident claim: a signed token carries its own claims (user ID, roles/scopes, expiry) such that any party holding the corresponding verification key can confirm the token is authentic and unmodified without needing to ask the issuing server again — trading a small amount of token size (claims travel with every request) for eliminating a database/session-store round trip on every request. The invariant protected is that a token's claims cannot be forged or altered without invalidating its signature, which is exactly why a JWT's payload, while not encrypted by default, is safe to trust for authorization decisions but must never contain secrets meant to stay hidden from the token holder.
sections.how_exactly: A user submits credentials to an authorization server (or a service acting as one) -> upon successful verification, the server issues a signed JWT access token containing claims (subject/user ID, roles or scopes, issued-at and expiry timestamps) -> the client includes this token on every subsequent request, typically as an `Authorization: Bearer <token>` header -> a receiving service's security filter (in Spring, a `SecurityFilterChain`/`OncePerRequestFilter`) intercepts the request before it reaches any Controller, extracts the token, verifies its signature against the known public key/shared secret (a fast, local cryptographic check — no network call needed), and checks its expiry -> if valid, the service extracts the claims and populates the request's security context (who this is, what they're allowed to do) -> Spring Security's method-level authorization (`@PreAuthorize`) or the Controller logic then checks those claims against what the specific action requires -> if the token is invalid, expired, or lacks the required scope, the request is rejected (401 or 403) before business logic ever runs.
sections.low_level_internals: A JWT is three base64url-encoded segments joined by dots: a header (algorithm, e.g. `HS256`/`RS256`), a payload (the claims, human-readable once decoded — never assume a JWT's contents are hidden from the holder, only that they're tamper-evident), and a signature (an HMAC over the header+payload using a shared secret, for `HS256`, or an RSA/ECDSA signature using a private key with a publicly-distributable verification key, for `RS256` — `RS256` is generally preferred across service boundaries since it lets any service verify tokens using only a public key, without ever holding the secret that could forge one). Verification is a local, offline cryptographic computation (no network call), which is precisely the performance property that makes JWTs attractive for high-throughput, multi-service systems compared to a session-store lookup on every request.
sections.who: The identity/authorization server (issuing and signing tokens), the client (storing and attaching the token to requests), each resource server's security filter (verifying signatures and extracting claims on every request), and, in an OIDC flow specifically, an identity provider distinct from the resource servers that ultimately consume the resulting tokens.
sections.industry: JWT/OAuth2/OIDC knowledge, and specifically the ability to explain the distinction between authentication and authorization precisely, is assumed baseline knowledge for any backend role and is frequently probed via 'walk me through what happens when a user logs in and then makes an authenticated API call' style questions.
sections.business: A broken or missing authorization check (as opposed to authentication) is one of the most common and severe classes of real security incident — a user being correctly authenticated as themselves but able to access another user's data due to a missing per-resource authorization check (an IDOR, insecure direct object reference) is a top-tier real-world vulnerability class, distinct from and more subtle than simply 'not requiring login at all.'
sections.product: Auth failures are maximally user-visible and trust-damaging when they go wrong in either direction — locking legitimate users out, or (far worse) letting a user see or modify data that isn't theirs.
sections.cost_economics: JWTs trade token size (larger than a simple session ID, since claims travel with every request) and the inability to instantly revoke a single already-issued token (it remains valid until its stated expiry, since there's no central lookup at verification time) against eliminating a database/session-store round trip on every single request — worth it at scale, and specifically why short expiry times plus a refresh-token flow are the standard mitigation for the revocation limitation.
sections.failure_incident: Symptom: a user can retrieve another user's private data by simply changing a resource ID in an otherwise-authenticated API request (e.g. `GET /orders/12345` returning someone else's order data when requested by a different, legitimately-logged-in user). Telemetry: the request succeeds with a 200 and valid-looking data despite the requesting user's ID not matching the resource's owner. Hypothesis: the endpoint correctly authenticates (verifies the JWT is valid) but never checks authorization (whether *this specific* authenticated user is allowed to access *this specific* resource). Diagnosis: code review confirms the Controller/Service checks token validity but not resource ownership. Root cause: authentication and authorization were conflated — a valid token was treated as sufficient for any action, rather than gating each specific resource access against the token's actual identity/claims. Fix: add an explicit per-resource ownership/scope check before returning or modifying any resource. Regression: a test asserting that User A's valid token cannot retrieve User B's resource, added specifically for every resource-owning endpoint. Business impact: a real data breach — one of the most damaging and reputation-costly categories of security incident, and one of the OWASP Top 10 (Broken Access Control).
sections.alternatives_tradeoffs: Server-side sessions (simple, instantly revocable, requires server-side state and doesn't scale as cleanly across many stateless services) vs. JWT access tokens (stateless, fast to verify, scales well across services, harder to revoke instantly — mitigated with short expiry + refresh tokens) vs. opaque tokens validated via a call to a central token-introspection endpoint (revocable instantly like a session, but reintroduces a network round trip on every verification, a deliberate trade toward revocability over the stateless-verification performance benefit).
sections.scenario: STUDY_SCENARIO: an API correctly requires a valid JWT for every request but never checks that the authenticated user's ID matches the resource being requested, allowing any logged-in user to read any other user's order by simply changing the ID in the URL (a textbook Broken Access Control / IDOR vulnerability). Explaining the precise distinction between authentication succeeding and authorization being entirely missing, and the specific per-resource ownership check that fixes it, is strong, realistic security interview material.

interview_mode.sec_15: Authentication proves who you are (login, token issuance); authorization decides what an already-authenticated identity is allowed to do — JWTs are a common way to carry the result of authentication (as signed claims) so authorization checks on later requests don't need a database lookup.
interview_mode.sec_30: A JWT is a signed, self-contained token whose claims can be verified locally (via signature check) without a network call, making it well-suited to stateless, multi-service architectures, at the cost of not being instantly revocable — mitigated with short expiry and refresh tokens. Authorization must still be checked explicitly per resource/action; a valid token alone only proves identity, not permission.
interview_mode.min_2: Explain the auth-vs-authz distinction precisely, walk the JWT verification flow (signature check, claims extraction, no network call), then use the IDOR/Broken Access Control incident (valid token, but no per-resource ownership check) as the concrete failure example, since it's the most common and instructive real-world way this whole area actually breaks.
interview_mode.deep_technical: Explain the difference between HS256 (shared-secret HMAC, both signing and verifying parties must hold the same secret) and RS256 (asymmetric, only the issuer holds the private signing key, any service can verify with the public key) and why RS256 is generally preferred across service boundaries.
interview_mode.system_design: Bring up short-lived access tokens plus longer-lived refresh tokens as the standard System Design answer to JWT's revocation limitation.
interview_mode.business_value: Emphasize Broken Access Control (OWASP Top 10) as one of the most damaging real vulnerability classes, precisely because authentication can be entirely correct while authorization is silently missing.
interview_mode.incident_debugging: Cite the specific diagnostic signature: a 200 response with correct-looking data for a resource the requesting authenticated user doesn't actually own — the fingerprint of missing per-resource authorization, not a broken login.

sections.current_status_2026: OAuth 2.1 (a consolidating, security-hardening revision of OAuth2's various RFCs, still finalizing as a formal spec but already reflected in current library defaults as of 2025-2026) removes several less-secure legacy flows (notably the Implicit flow) and mandates PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange) even for confidential clients, reflecting hard-won lessons about token-interception vulnerabilities in the original OAuth2 spec. Passkeys/WebAuthn (passwordless, public-key-based authentication) have become an increasingly mainstream authentication method alongside, not replacing, the OAuth2/OIDC/JWT authorization layer described above.

domains.title: Testing / Quality
domains.short_overview: The layered discipline of verifying a change is genuinely correct before it reaches production, and why an implementer's own say-so is never sufficient evidence alone.

children.title: Testing Strategy: The Test Pyramid & Independent Verification
children.short_overview: Why different test types exist at different layers, in different proportions, and why a test suite an implementer writes for their own change is weaker evidence than independent verification.

sections.why: A coherent testing strategy is what lets a team ship changes confidently and fast rather than either shipping blind or manually re-verifying everything by hand on every change — and 'how do you decide what to test and at what level' is a standard senior engineering interview question testing judgment, not just familiarity with a test framework. This project's own multi-layer suite (Python, Node/Playwright E2E, Java/JUnit, plus an explicitly independent qa-evaluator) is real, demonstrated current project experience of exactly this strategy.
sections.history_evolution: The Test Pyramid concept (Mike Cohn, in his 2009 book 'Succeeding with Agile') formalized the intuition that a healthy test suite should have many fast, cheap unit tests at the base, fewer integration tests in the middle, and very few slow, expensive end-to-end tests at the top — a direct reaction against the earlier, common anti-pattern of relying primarily on slow, brittle manual or UI-driven end-to-end tests (sometimes derided as an 'ice cream cone' anti-pattern, the pyramid inverted). Test-Driven Development (Kent Beck, formalized and popularized starting around 2000 as part of Extreme Programming) contributed the discipline of writing a failing test before the code that makes it pass, though it's a development practice distinct from the pyramid's structural guidance on test-type proportions.
sections.why_now: A full pyramid is justified for any system expected to change repeatedly over time by more than one person (or by an AI agent making autonomous changes, this project's own core use case) — the whole point is confidence that a change didn't break something else, cheaply and repeatably. For a genuine one-off throwaway script, extensive testing infrastructure is unjustified overhead.
sections.big_picture: Business requirement: changes can be shipped repeatedly without an escalating manual-verification burden, and defects are caught before reaching production rather than being discovered by customers. Architecture: unit tests verify a single function/class in isolation (fast, numerous); integration tests verify that multiple real components work together correctly (e.g. a Repository against a real, if lightweight, database); end-to-end/browser tests verify a full user journey through the actual running system (slow, few, but catch classes of bug (wiring, real network calls, actual rendered UI) no lower layer can).
sections.design_intellect: The core idea is a cost/confidence trade-off by layer: a unit test is cheap to write and run and pinpoints a failure precisely, but proves nothing about whether components actually integrate correctly; an end-to-end test proves the whole system genuinely works together as a user would experience it, but is slow, more brittle (many more moving parts that can cause an unrelated failure), and doesn't pinpoint the root cause as precisely. The pyramid shape (many unit, fewer integration, fewest E2E) is the practical answer to using each layer for what it's uniquely good at while minimizing total cost — and independent QA (a separate evaluator checking the implementer's claimed result against real evidence, rather than trusting the implementer's own tests) exists because an implementer's tests reflect the implementer's own understanding of the requirement, which can share the exact same blind spot as the implementation itself.
sections.how_exactly: A change is made to a Service method -> a unit test exercises that method directly with mocked/fake dependencies, verifying its logic in isolation, running in milliseconds -> an integration test exercises the Repository layer against a real (if lightweight, e.g. H2 in-memory) database, verifying the actual SQL/JPA mapping is correct, running in tens to hundreds of milliseconds -> an end-to-end/Playwright test drives a real browser against the actually-running full application (frontend + backend + database), verifying the complete user-visible journey, running in seconds -> after all deterministic layers pass, an independent evaluator (this project's own qa-evaluator subagent) re-examines the change against its original Acceptance Contract using only Read/Glob/Grep/Bash/WebFetch tools (no ability to modify anything), specifically to avoid the implementer's own confirmation bias about whether the requirement was actually met.
sections.low_level_internals: Unit tests typically run entirely in-process with no I/O (mocked dependencies), making them CPU-bound and extremely fast; integration tests incur real I/O (an actual, if local, database connection and query execution); E2E/browser tests incur real network round trips, real rendering, and real timing/async behavior (which is exactly why they need explicit waits/assertions with generous timeouts rather than fixed sleeps, to avoid flakiness from timing assumptions that don't hold under load or on a slower CI runner).
sections.who: The implementer (writing unit/integration tests as part of the change itself), a CI pipeline or local test runner (executing the full pyramid deterministically), a browser automation engine (Playwright, driving real E2E journeys), and an independent reviewer/evaluator (verifying the claimed result against real evidence rather than the implementer's own say-so).
sections.industry: The Test Pyramid remains the standard reference model cited in essentially every engineering-culture discussion of testing strategy industry-wide; 'how would you test this feature' (expecting a multi-layer answer, not just 'I'd write unit tests') is a common interview question at every seniority level.
sections.business: A shallow or unbalanced test suite (e.g. only E2E tests, or only unit tests with no integration coverage) either lets real integration bugs reach production (missing integration layer) or makes the suite so slow and brittle that engineers start skipping it under deadline pressure (too much E2E) — both directly increase the rate of production incidents and erode delivery velocity over time.
sections.product: A well-tested product ships new features with fewer regressions in unrelated areas — testing strategy is largely invisible to a product manager until its absence causes a visible, embarrassing regression in production.
sections.cost_economics: Each layer has a different cost-per-run and cost-per-defect-caught; the pyramid shape specifically minimizes total testing cost for a given level of confidence by pushing as much verification as possible down to the cheapest layer that can actually catch a given class of bug, reserving the expensive E2E layer for what only E2E can verify (real wiring, real user journeys).
sections.failure_incident: Symptom: a change passes all of its own unit tests but breaks a real user journey in production. Telemetry: no test failure anywhere in CI, but a real production error or user complaint. Hypothesis: the change's own tests only verified the changed unit in isolation and never exercised the actual integration point (a different component's assumption about the changed unit's behavior) that broke. Diagnosis: reproducing the user journey manually reveals the gap immediately; the missing coverage is at the integration or E2E layer, not the unit layer. Root cause: an unbalanced test suite (heavy on unit tests for the specific function changed, no integration/E2E coverage for how it's actually used elsewhere). Fix: add the missing integration or E2E test covering the actual broken journey, and, for the specific bug, a regression test asserting the exact previously-broken behavior. Regression: exactly this new test, permanently preventing recurrence. Business impact: a production defect that a correctly-shaped test suite (or independent QA) would have caught before release.
sections.alternatives_tradeoffs: Heavy unit testing with light integration/E2E (fast feedback, but risks integration/wiring bugs slipping through, since units passing in isolation says nothing about them working together) vs. heavy E2E testing with light unit coverage (the 'ice cream cone' anti-pattern — high confidence when it passes, but slow, brittle, and imprecise about root cause on failure) vs. a genuinely balanced pyramid (the standard, generally-correct default) vs. relying solely on the implementer's own tests without independent verification (faster, but shares the implementer's own blind spots and lacks a genuinely adversarial check).

interview_mode.sec_15: A test pyramid uses many fast, cheap unit tests at the base, fewer integration tests verifying real component interaction in the middle, and very few slow end-to-end tests verifying full real user journeys at the top — each layer catches a different class of bug at a different cost.
interview_mode.sec_30: Unit tests are cheap and pinpoint failures precisely but prove nothing about integration; E2E tests prove the whole system genuinely works together but are slow and imprecise about root cause — the pyramid shape uses each layer for what it's uniquely good at while minimizing total testing cost and time. Independent QA (someone other than the implementer verifying the result against real evidence) exists specifically because an implementer's own tests share the implementer's own blind spots about the requirement.
interview_mode.min_2: Explain the pyramid's cost/confidence trade-off by layer with concrete examples (unit test on a Service method, integration test against a real lightweight database, E2E test driving a real browser through the full stack), then explain why independent verification is a distinct, additional layer beyond the pyramid itself, using this project's own qa-evaluator (read-only tools, no ability to modify code, checking claimed results against real evidence) as a concrete real example.
interview_mode.deep_technical: Explain why E2E tests need explicit condition-based waits rather than fixed sleeps, given real async/network timing variance across environments (local vs. CI, different machine speeds).
interview_mode.system_design: Frame testing strategy as itself a System Design decision proportional to how often and by whom (including AI agents) a system will be changed — more autonomous or frequent change justifies more automated verification layers.
interview_mode.business_value: Connect an unbalanced test suite directly to either slower delivery (too much slow E2E, discouraging frequent testing) or more production incidents (too little integration/E2E coverage) — both are real, measurable costs.
interview_mode.incident_debugging: Use the 'passed all unit tests, broke in production' incident shape to illustrate exactly what a missing integration/E2E layer looks like when it fails.

sections.current_status_2026: Contract testing (e.g. Pact) has become a more mainstream middle-layer addition in 2026 microservices architectures specifically to catch breaking API changes between independently-deployed services without needing full E2E environments for every combination — a direct answer to the scaling challenge of E2E testing across many services. AI-assisted test generation is increasingly common but is explicitly not a substitute for independent, adversarial verification of the resulting change, per this project's own established practice.

domains.title: Observability / Production
domains.short_overview: Being able to answer 'what is this system actually doing right now, and why' from real captured evidence, and the incident-response discipline built on top of it.

children.title: Observability: Logs, Metrics, Traces & SLIs/SLOs
children.short_overview: The difference between monitoring (knowing something is wrong) and observability (being able to ask why, from data already being captured), and the SLI/SLO framework for defining 'working' precisely.

sections.why: A production system without real observability leaves an operator unable to answer 'is it working right now, and if not, why' from evidence — forcing guesswork during exactly the highest-pressure moments (an active incident). This is consistently tested in senior/staff interviews via incident-response and production-readiness questions, and this project's own event ledger, structured metrics, and safe-trace logging are genuine, demonstrated current project experience.
sections.history_evolution: Traditional monitoring (Nagios, and similar tools, 1990s-2000s) focused on predefined health checks and threshold alerts on known failure modes. The term 'observability,' borrowed from control theory (a system is observable if its internal state can be inferred from its external outputs), was popularized for software specifically by engineers at companies like Twitter and Honeycomb (Charity Majors, co-founder, a leading voice from the mid-2010s onward) as a reaction to monitoring's limits in genuinely novel, complex distributed-systems failures that no predefined dashboard or alert was built to anticipate. OpenTelemetry (a 2019 CNCF merger of the earlier competing OpenTracing and OpenCensus projects) has since become the vendor-neutral industry-standard instrumentation API for logs, metrics, and traces together.
sections.why_now: Justified for any system where an operator needs to understand real runtime behavior after deployment — which is essentially any production service. Minimal for a short-lived local script with a human directly watching its output the whole time.
sections.big_picture: Business requirement: an operator can determine, from real captured evidence (not guessing or trusting a status page's own self-report), whether the system is currently healthy, and if not, diagnose why quickly enough to limit business impact. NFR: Service Level Indicators (SLIs, e.g. p99 latency, error rate) measured continuously, compared against Service Level Objectives (SLOs, an internal target, e.g. '99.9% of requests succeed within 500ms'), which in turn may underlie an external Service Level Agreement (SLA, a contractual commitment) with real financial consequences if violated.
sections.design_intellect: The core idea is capturing enough structured, correlatable data at the time an event happens (not reconstructing it after the fact from guesswork) that any question an operator might later need to ask ('what did this specific request actually do,' 'is this degradation isolated to one component or system-wide') can be answered from already-captured evidence — the specific mechanism (a correlation ID, like this project's own run_id/session_id, attached to every event belonging to one logical operation) is what makes reconstructing a full request's trajectory possible after the fact from otherwise-independent log lines.
sections.how_exactly: A request enters the system -> a correlation/trace ID is generated (or propagated, if the caller already supplied one) and attached to every subsequent log line, metric emission, and downstream call this request triggers -> logs record discrete, timestamped facts about what happened (this project's own safe trace deliberately narrows this to tool name, sanitized input, and status, to guarantee secrets never leak into a log) -> metrics aggregate numeric measurements over time (request counts, durations, error rates) into a queryable time series -> traces (where implemented) follow the request's path across every component/service it touches, showing where time was actually spent -> an SLI is computed continuously from this data (e.g. p99 latency from the metrics stream) and compared against its SLO target -> when an SLO is at risk of being violated, an alert fires, ideally before a customer-visible SLA breach occurs, giving the operator time to react from already-available diagnostic data rather than starting from zero.
sections.low_level_internals: A metric is typically stored as a time series (a sequence of timestamped numeric values, often pre-aggregated into buckets/percentiles rather than storing every raw event, to bound storage cost at high volume); a distributed trace is a tree of timed spans, each representing one unit of work (e.g. one service call) with a parent-child relationship showing causality and where latency accumulated across the whole request's path. Correlation IDs are typically propagated via a request header (e.g. `traceparent`, the W3C Trace Context standard) so every service in a call chain can attach its own spans/logs to the same overall trace, regardless of which service actually generated the ID.
sections.who: The application code (emitting structured logs/metrics/spans at meaningful points), an observability backend (aggregating and indexing this data for query — e.g. this project's own event ledger, or a commercial APM tool), an operator/on-call engineer (querying this data during normal operation and especially during an incident), and, where implemented, an alerting system (comparing SLIs against SLOs and notifying humans when thresholds are crossed).
sections.industry: 'How would you know if this system is degraded, and how would you find out why' is a staple senior/staff System Design and production-readiness interview question; SLI/SLO/SLA vocabulary (popularized industry-wide by Google's Site Reliability Engineering book, 2016) is assumed baseline knowledge for any role with production ownership.
sections.business: Without real observability, the first sign of a problem is often a customer complaint or a revenue drop noticed well after the fact — observability investment directly reduces both the detection time and the diagnosis time of an incident, both of which are the primary levers controlling an incident's total business cost.
sections.product: Product decisions (which feature to invest in next) are frequently informed by usage metrics that are a direct byproduct of the same observability instrumentation built for operational health — a well-instrumented system serves both purposes from the same underlying data.
sections.cost_economics: Observability data has a real storage/processing cost that scales with volume — the practical answer (sampling for high-volume traces, pre-aggregation for metrics, careful log-level discipline) trades some fidelity for bounded cost, an explicit and necessary engineering decision rather than 'capture everything forever.'
sections.failure_incident: Symptom: users report the system is slow, but no dashboard or alert had fired, and the on-call engineer has no data to start from. Telemetry: none, or only coarse, non-granular metrics that don't isolate which component or request type is actually affected. Hypothesis: observability coverage has a genuine gap (an SLI was never defined for this specific user journey, or a critical component emits no metrics/traces at all). Diagnosis: the incident is eventually resolved only via manual reproduction and code-level debugging, taking far longer than it would have with proper instrumentation. Root cause: an observability gap identified only in retrospect, during the postmortem. Fix: add the missing SLI/metric/trace instrumentation for this specific class of request, plus an alert on its SLO. Regression: for observability specifically, the 'regression test' is the postmortem action item itself — a durable commitment (tracked in a document, this project's own LESSONS.md/ACTION_QUEUE.json convention) to close the specific gap, verified in a later audit. Business impact: an incident's total cost is dominated by detection-and-diagnosis time when observability is missing, often far exceeding what the underlying bug itself would have cost to simply fix once found.
sections.alternatives_tradeoffs: Full distributed tracing (best diagnostic power for complex multi-service systems, real cost and complexity to instrument and store) vs. metrics + structured logs only (cheaper, sufficient for a simpler or single-process system, harder to follow a request across multiple services) vs. minimal ad hoc logging (cheapest up front, effectively guarantees a slow, painful incident investigation the first time something genuinely goes wrong) vs. commercial APM platforms (fast to adopt, real recurring cost, often the pragmatic choice for a team without dedicated observability engineering capacity).

interview_mode.sec_15: Observability means being able to answer why a system is behaving a certain way from already-captured logs, metrics, and traces, rather than guessing — SLIs are the measured indicators (like p99 latency), SLOs are the internal targets for them, and SLAs are external contractual commitments built on top.
interview_mode.sec_30: The key design principle is capturing enough structured, correlatable data (via a correlation/trace ID attached to every log line and metric for one logical request) at the time something happens that any later question can be answered from existing evidence, rather than needing to reproduce the problem to understand it after the fact.
interview_mode.min_2: Explain the logs/metrics/traces distinction and the SLI/SLO/SLA hierarchy, then walk an incident where missing observability (no SLI defined for the affected journey) forced a slow manual investigation, contrasted with how a correlation-ID-based trace would have made the same diagnosis immediate.
interview_mode.deep_technical: Explain how a distributed trace's span tree captures causality and per-hop latency across multiple services, and why correlation IDs must be propagated via request headers (e.g. W3C Trace Context) rather than regenerated per service.
interview_mode.system_design: Bring up SLO-driven alerting (alert before an SLA is breached, not just when something is already fully broken) as a specific, senior-level System Design detail most junior designs omit entirely.
interview_mode.business_value: State plainly that an incident's total business cost is usually dominated by detection-and-diagnosis time, not fix time — making observability investment one of the highest-leverage reliability investments available.
interview_mode.incident_debugging: Use the 'no dashboard fired, no data to start from' symptom as the textbook signature of an observability gap, distinct from a well-instrumented incident where the data exists but hasn't yet been looked at.

sections.current_status_2026: OpenTelemetry is now the de facto standard instrumentation API across the industry in 2026 for logs, metrics, and traces together, with most major APM vendors (Datadog, Honeycomb, Grafana/Tempo) supporting it natively rather than requiring vendor-specific SDKs — meaning instrumentation code is increasingly vendor-neutral and portable between backends, a significant maturation since observability tooling fragmented across incompatible vendor SDKs in the early-to-mid 2010s.

children.title: Safe Deployment & Rollback Strategy
children.short_overview: How to ship a change to production without betting the whole system on it working correctly the first time, and how to reliably undo it if it doesn't.

sections.why: Deployment is the single moment a system is most likely to break, because it's the one point where the running system genuinely changes — a deliberate, safe deployment strategy (and a proven rollback path) is what turns 'we hope this works' into 'we know within minutes if it doesn't, and can undo it immediately.' This project's own real practice (independent production verification of the actual requested effect, not just a green deploy-command exit code) is genuine current project experience.
sections.history_evolution: Early web deployment was often a manual, high-risk 'stop the server, copy new files, start the server' process with real downtime and no easy undo. Blue-green deployment (running two full production environments, switching traffic between them, popularized industry-wide through the 2000s-2010s as infrastructure automation matured) made instant rollback possible by simply switching traffic back. Canary deployment (named after the coal-mine canary, releasing a change to a small fraction of traffic/users first) let teams detect a bad change from real production signal before it affects everyone, popularized heavily by Google's and Netflix's public engineering practices in the 2010s. Feature flags (decoupling code deployment from feature activation, widely adopted through the 2010s via tools like LaunchDarkly) further split 'is the new code running' from 'is the new behavior turned on,' allowing instant behavioral rollback without a full redeploy.
sections.why_now: Needed for any system where downtime or a bad release has real user/business impact — which is essentially any live production service. Overkill (blue-green infrastructure, canary tooling) for a low-traffic internal tool where a brief manual restart on failure is genuinely an acceptable cost.
sections.big_picture: Business requirement: a deployment either clearly succeeds (verified by its actual requested effect being live, not merely a process starting) or is safely and quickly reverted, minimizing the duration any user is exposed to a broken system. Architecture: the deployment pipeline itself, plus an explicit, tested rollback path (a previous known-good version that can actually still be deployed, not just theoretically 'still exists in git').
sections.design_intellect: The core idea is treating 'did the deploy actually work' as a question that must be answered by evidence of the deploy's specific intended effect being observably true in the live system, not by a deploy tool's own exit code or 'Online' status — a deploy command can report success while the actual desired change (e.g. a new endpoint behaving correctly, a bug fix genuinely fixed) is not yet true, due to caching, a stale build, a partial rollout, or the tool's own status reporting being decoupled from real application health. The invariant a good rollback strategy protects is that reverting is always genuinely possible quickly — which requires the previous version to still be a real, deployable artifact, not just a git commit that's since drifted from what's actually deployable (missing a dependency version that's no longer available, for instance).
sections.how_exactly: Code is committed and pushed -> a deployment is triggered (this project's own convention: `railway up`) -> the deploy tool reports a status (built, started, 'Online') -> this status alone is treated as necessary but explicitly insufficient evidence of success -> independent verification then checks the actual live requested effect (e.g. fetching the specific new endpoint and confirming its real behavior, not just that the server responds with any HTTP 200) -> if verification passes, the deployment is considered genuinely complete; if it fails, the team either fixes forward quickly or rolls back to the last known-good deployable version -> a rollback re-deploys that previous version through the same pipeline, and is itself re-verified the same way, since even a rollback can fail.
sections.low_level_internals: A 'successful' deploy command exit code typically only confirms the artifact was built and the process started listening on its port — it says nothing about downstream effects like a stale CDN/browser cache serving old assets, a database migration not yet applied, or a load balancer still routing some traffic to an old instance during a rolling deploy — each of these is a distinct way a technically-successful deploy can still leave the actual user-visible system in a broken or inconsistent state for a period of time.
sections.who: The engineer/AI agent triggering the deployment, the deployment platform (Railway, Kubernetes, etc., executing the build/start/health-check lifecycle), a load balancer or router (directing traffic, potentially gradually during a canary/rolling deploy), and an independent verifier (human or, in this project's case, a distinct evaluator) confirming the actual live effect rather than trusting the deploy tool's own report.
sections.industry: 'Never trust a green deploy status alone — verify the actual effect' is widely repeated senior/staff engineering wisdom, usually learned the hard way from a real incident where a 'successful' deployment didn't actually fix or ship what was intended.
sections.business: A bad deployment that isn't caught and reverted quickly directly extends the duration of user-facing impact — the entire point of canary/blue-green/feature-flag strategies is bounding that duration and blast radius as tightly as possible, which is a direct, quantifiable reduction in incident cost.
sections.product: Users should ideally never be able to tell a deployment happened at all (true zero-downtime, gradually-verified rollout) — any user-visible deployment friction (a brief error spike, a jarring behavior change) is a sign the deployment strategy itself has room to improve.
sections.cost_economics: Blue-green/canary infrastructure has a real cost (running duplicate or partial-capacity environments temporarily) that buys a dramatically reduced blast radius and rollback time for a bad change — worth it once the cost of a bad deployment reaching all users clearly exceeds the infrastructure cost of a safer rollout strategy.
sections.failure_incident: Symptom: a deployment reports success ('Online,' HTTP 200 on a health check) but the actual feature/fix it was meant to ship isn't working correctly in production. Telemetry: the deploy tool's own status is green; a specific, targeted check of the actual intended behavior fails. Hypothesis: a stale build was deployed (an old cached layer, a build that silently used cached dependencies), or the health check itself is too shallow (just 'process is up') to detect the real problem. Diagnosis: comparing the deployed artifact's actual content/behavior against what was intended reveals the mismatch. Root cause: the verification step trusted the deploy tool's status as sufficient evidence, rather than independently confirming the real requested effect. Fix: add (or use) a verification step that checks the actual specific behavior after every deployment, not just process health, before declaring the deployment complete. Regression: this verification step itself becomes a permanent, repeated part of the deployment process for every future deployment. Business impact: users experiencing a supposedly-fixed bug that was never actually fixed in production, and a team believing (incorrectly) that the issue was resolved.
sections.alternatives_tradeoffs: Blue-green (instant, safe rollback by traffic switch, doubles infrastructure cost during the switch window) vs. canary (gradual, safest for catching subtle issues from real traffic before full exposure, more complex to implement and monitor) vs. rolling deployment (no extra infrastructure, but a period where old and new versions run simultaneously, requiring backward/forward compatibility during the transition) vs. simple stop-and-replace (simplest, real downtime, acceptable only for low-traffic/low-criticality systems) — each paired with feature flags as an orthogonal, additional lever for instant behavioral rollback independent of code deployment.

interview_mode.sec_15: A deploy tool reporting success only confirms the process started — the actual deployment is only genuinely complete once the specific intended effect is independently verified live, and a safe strategy (blue-green/canary/rolling) bounds how many users are exposed to a bad change before it's caught and reverted.
interview_mode.sec_30: Never trust a green deploy status alone: a technically-successful deploy can still leave the real user-visible system broken (stale cache, unapplied migration, partial rollout) — the fix is always independent verification of the actual requested effect, plus a deployment strategy (canary, blue-green) that limits blast radius and a rollback path that's genuinely still deployable, not just theoretically present in git history.
interview_mode.min_2: Walk the 'green deploy, broken feature' incident end to end, then explain canary/blue-green/rolling as three different ways to bound exposure to a bad change, and feature flags as an orthogonal lever for instant behavioral rollback without a full redeploy.
interview_mode.deep_technical: Explain the specific ways a 'successful' deploy status can diverge from real correctness: stale CDN/browser cache, an unapplied database migration, or a rolling deploy leaving old and new versions serving simultaneously.
interview_mode.system_design: Bring up feature flags as decoupling 'is the code deployed' from 'is the behavior active,' a distinct and complementary System Design lever to the deployment strategy itself.
interview_mode.business_value: State plainly that the entire purpose of these strategies is bounding the duration and blast radius of a bad change, a directly quantifiable reduction in incident cost.
interview_mode.incident_debugging: Use 'deploy tool said success, actual feature is broken' as the textbook signature that verification was insufficiently deep.

sections.current_status_2026: Progressive delivery (the combined discipline of canary + feature flags + automated rollback triggered by real-time SLO monitoring, rather than a human watching a dashboard) is the current state-of-the-art framing in 2026 industry practice, with tools like Argo Rollouts and Flagger automating the canary-analysis-and-promote-or-rollback decision itself based on live metrics.

children.title: Artificial Intelligence
children.short_overview: Computer systems performing tasks that normally require human intelligence — perception, reasoning, language, decision-making.

sections.what: The general field of building systems that perform tasks normally requiring human intelligence: perception, language, reasoning, planning, decision-making.
sections.why: The umbrella term matters less than knowing where a specific system actually sits within it -- AI ranges from a hand-written if/else rules engine to a trillion-parameter neural network, and interviewers probe whether a candidate can tell the difference rather than treating 'AI' as one monolithic thing.
sections.how: In practice today, 'AI' in a backend engineering context almost always means either classical machine learning (a model trained on labeled data for a narrow task) or a large language model (trained on broad text/code, used via API, capable of open-ended generation and tool use).
sections.when: Use the general term only when scoping a conversation broadly (e.g. 'AI strategy'); in any technical discussion, name the specific technique (LLM, embedding model, classifier) instead -- 'AI' alone is too vague to be checkable.
sections.context: This project deliberately draws a hard, documented line between deterministic code (decides truth/authorization/routing) and LLM calls (used only for genuine semantic synthesis) -- see docs/CONSTITUTION.md and every Deterministic vs LLM panel across this app's own pages.

interview.question: How do you define 'AI' when a non-technical stakeholder uses the term loosely?
interview.short_answer: I ask what specific capability they mean -- classification, generation, retrieval, planning -- because 'AI' alone doesn't tell you which of several very different engineering approaches applies.
interview.deep_answer: Treating 'AI' as one thing is the single most common source of unrealistic expectations in a project: a stakeholder who has seen a chatbot assumes a classifier can 'just understand' their request, or that an LLM can guarantee deterministic correctness. Part of the engineering job is translating a vague AI request into the actual mechanism (rules engine, ML classifier, LLM with retrieval, LLM with tool use) and its real, honest capability and failure boundary.

children.title: Machine Learning
children.short_overview: Systems that improve at a task from data/experience rather than being explicitly programmed with rules for every case.

sections.what: Systems that improve at a task by learning statistical patterns from data, rather than following explicitly hand-coded rules for every case.
sections.why: The core trade-off a backend engineer must reason about: a rules engine is fully predictable and debuggable but brittle to unanticipated input; an ML model generalizes to unseen input but its behavior on any single case is a probability, not a guarantee.
sections.how: A model is trained on historical examples (features -> labels), producing learned parameters; at inference time, the same feature-extraction is applied to new input and the model outputs a prediction -- classification, regression, ranking, or (for generative models) new content.
sections.when: Reach for classical ML when the task is a well-defined, narrow prediction with enough labeled data (fraud scoring, churn prediction, spam classification) -- reach for an LLM instead when the task is open-ended language/code understanding or generation with no practical way to hand-label enough training examples.
sections.context: This project has no classical ML models of its own (no training pipeline, no labeled dataset) -- its 'AI' surface is entirely LLM-API-based (Claude), a deliberate scope decision honestly reflected in its own capability registry rather than claimed as something it doesn't have.

interview.question: When would you choose a traditional ML model over an LLM for a backend feature?
interview.short_answer: When the task is narrow, well-defined, and you have (or can get) real labeled data -- a purpose-built classifier will be cheaper, faster, and more predictable than an LLM call for that exact narrow task.
interview.deep_answer: LLMs are general-purpose and require no training data of your own, which makes them fast to prototype with -- but for a genuinely narrow, high-volume, latency-sensitive task (e.g. real-time fraud scoring on every transaction), a small trained classifier is usually cheaper per-call, faster, and has a much smaller, more auditable failure surface than routing every request through a general-purpose LLM.

children.title: Deep Learning
children.short_overview: Machine learning using multi-layer neural networks to learn hierarchical representations directly from raw data.

sections.what: A subfield of machine learning using multi-layer neural networks to learn hierarchical representations directly from raw data (pixels, text tokens, audio) rather than requiring hand-engineered features.
sections.why: Deep learning is what made today's large language models possible -- understanding roughly how it works (layers, weights, gradient-based training) demystifies what an LLM API call is actually doing on the other end, rather than treating it as an unexplainable black box.
sections.how: Data flows forward through stacked layers of learned weighted connections (a forward pass) producing a prediction; the error between prediction and ground truth is propagated backward (backpropagation) to adjust every weight slightly in the direction that reduces future error, repeated over millions of examples.
sections.when: Relevant to a backend engineer mainly as context for reasoning about LLM behavior/limits (why they hallucinate, why more parameters/data generally helps but isn't a guarantee, why fine-tuning is expensive) -- actually training deep networks is a distinct specialization most backend/full-stack engineers will never do hands-on.
sections.context: Not something this project trains or fine-tunes -- it consumes pre-trained foundation models (Claude) entirely via API, which is the correct, honest scope for an application-layer engineering project.

interview.question: You don't train models yourself -- how do you reason about an LLM's behavior without that background?
interview.short_answer: I treat the model as a real but imperfect statistical predictor of the next token given context, not magic -- that framing explains hallucination, context-length limits, and why grounding retrieved evidence matters, without needing to have trained one myself.
interview.deep_answer: You don't need to have trained a model to reason correctly about its behavior at the API level -- what matters operationally is knowing it's a probabilistic function of its input context, that longer/more relevant context generally improves output quality up to a point, that it has no persistent memory between calls unless you provide it, and that its stated confidence is not a reliable signal of correctness. Those facts drive real engineering decisions (context engineering, groundedness checking, independent verification) regardless of training-level expertise.

children.title: Neural Networks
children.short_overview: Layered networks of simple weighted units (neurons) whose connection strengths are learned from data via backpropagation.

sections.what: A computational model of interconnected 'neurons' (weighted sums followed by a non-linear activation function) organized in layers, which together can approximate very complex functions.
sections.why: The building block of every deep learning system, including the transformer architecture behind modern LLMs -- understanding a single neuron/layer is the foundation for understanding attention, embeddings, and why models need so much data and compute.
sections.how: Each neuron computes a weighted sum of its inputs plus a bias, passes the result through a non-linear activation function (historically sigmoid/tanh, now mostly variants of ReLU or GELU) -- non-linearity is what lets stacked layers represent complex, non-linear relationships rather than collapsing to a single linear transformation.
sections.when: Interview-relevant mainly as foundational vocabulary (weights, biases, activation functions, layers) that shows up when discussing why LLMs behave the way they do, not something typically implemented from scratch in application engineering work.
sections.context: N/A -- conceptual/foundational knowledge, not something this project implements directly (it consumes a pre-trained model via API).

interview.question: What does 'the model has billions of parameters' actually mean?
interview.short_answer: Each parameter is one learned weight or bias inside the network's neurons -- billions of them means billions of individually-tuned numbers that together encode the patterns the model learned from its training data.
interview.deep_answer: More parameters generally give a model more capacity to represent complex patterns, which is part of why larger models tend to perform better on a wide range of tasks -- but parameter count alone doesn't determine quality; training data quality/quantity, architecture choices, and post-training (RLHF, instruction tuning) all matter enormously too. A well-trained smaller model can outperform a poorly-trained larger one.

children.title: Generative AI
children.short_overview: Models that produce new content (text, code, images) rather than only classifying or scoring existing input.

sections.what: AI systems that produce new content (text, code, images, audio) rather than only classifying or scoring existing input -- the category modern LLMs belong to.
sections.why: Generative AI is the specific capability that makes LLM-assisted software delivery possible (generating code, explanations, test cases) -- distinguishing it from discriminative/classification AI clarifies what an LLM is actually good at (producing plausible, contextually-appropriate new content) versus what it is not inherently good at (guaranteeing factual correctness or determinism).
sections.how: A generative model learns the statistical distribution of its training data well enough to sample new, coherent outputs from that distribution -- an LLM specifically generates text one token at a time, each token sampled based on the probability distribution the model computes over its entire vocabulary given everything before it.
sections.when: Reach for generative AI when the task genuinely requires producing novel content (a draft explanation, a candidate code change, a summarization) -- not for tasks with a single correct deterministic answer, where deterministic code is faster, cheaper, and more reliable.
sections.context: This project's own explicit design law, stated in its Role Showcase and enforced structurally in agent/reasoning_gateway.py: deterministic where truth is computable, LLM only for genuine semantic synthesis.

interview.question: How do you decide whether a feature genuinely needs generative AI?
interview.short_answer: I ask whether the correct answer can be computed deterministically from data I already have -- if yes, generative AI adds cost, latency, and a new failure mode for no benefit; if the task genuinely requires producing novel, context-appropriate content, that's the real signal to use it.
interview.deep_answer: This project applied that exact test when building its public 'Ask the Codebase' feature: retrieval alone (real cosine-similarity search over pre-embedded chunks) was sufficient to answer 'where is X handled?' honestly and accurately, so it deliberately makes zero LLM calls -- adding generative AI there would have introduced unbounded cost, a prompt-injection surface, and a place for a confident-sounding wrong answer, for zero real benefit over retrieval alone.
interview.real_incident_story: See docs/interview-scenarios/11-ask-the-codebase.md's own explicit design-law section for the real reasoning behind this specific zero-LLM decision.

children.title: Foundation Models
children.short_overview: Large models pre-trained on broad data, then adapted (via prompting or fine-tuning) to many downstream tasks — e.g. Claude.

sections.what: Very large models pre-trained on broad, diverse data (text, code, sometimes images) that serve as a general-purpose base, later adaptable to many downstream tasks via prompting or fine-tuning -- e.g. Claude, GPT, Gemini.
sections.why: Understanding that today's LLMs are 'foundation models' explains why one API can handle wildly different tasks (coding, summarization, analysis, conversation) without task-specific retraining -- the model's broad pre-training gives it general capability, and prompting/context steers that capability toward a specific task at inference time.
sections.how: Trained at enormous scale (often trillions of tokens) using self-supervised objectives (predicting the next token, or masked-token prediction), then typically further refined via instruction tuning and RLHF (reinforcement learning from human feedback) to make outputs more helpful, honest, and harmless before public release.
sections.when: Relevant whenever choosing or reasoning about which model to use for a task -- foundation model capability, training cutoff, context window, and cost/latency profile are all real, checkable properties that should drive the choice, not brand familiarity alone.
sections.context: This project's own model/effort selection policy (recorded in the private karthik-ai-context repo, not fabricated capabilities) explicitly verifies real product capabilities (model aliases, effort levels) against the live CLI/schema before configuring anything, after an earlier research pass gave incorrect information about what was actually available.

interview.question: How do you evaluate which foundation model to use for a given task?
interview.short_answer: Real, verified capability against the actual task (context window, tool-use support, coding benchmark performance), cost/latency trade-offs, and -- critically -- verifying claims against the live product/API rather than trusting documentation or a general research pass that might be stale or wrong.
interview.deep_answer: A real mistake caught in this exact project: an earlier research pass claimed a 'best' model alias existed and that certain effort-level values were valid, both factually wrong -- caught only by directly running the CLI's own help output and checking the real settings schema before writing any configuration. The general lesson: for fast-moving foundation-model products, verify current capability against the live system, never trust a cached mental model of what's available.

domains.title: LLMs
domains.short_overview: Reference index — 10 topic(s) migrated from the original Learn catalog.

children.title: Transformer
children.short_overview: The neural network architecture (attention-based, no recurrence) underlying modern large language models.

sections.what: The neural network architecture (Vaswani et al., 2017, 'Attention Is All You Need') behind every modern LLM -- processes an entire input sequence in parallel using self-attention, rather than one token at a time like older recurrent networks.
sections.why: Parallel processing made training on internet-scale data feasible, and self-attention lets the model directly relate any two tokens in its context regardless of distance -- both are why transformers, not RNNs, power today's LLMs.
sections.how: Stacked layers, each combining a self-attention sub-layer (lets every token 'look at' every other token and weigh their relevance) with a feed-forward sub-layer, plus residual connections and normalization for stable training at depth.
sections.when: Foundational vocabulary for any conversation about LLM internals, context windows, or why certain tasks (long-range reasoning across a large document) are easier or harder for the model.
sections.context: N/A -- this project consumes a pre-trained transformer (Claude) via API; does not implement transformer internals.

interview.question: Why did transformers replace RNNs for language modeling?
interview.short_answer: Self-attention processes a whole sequence in parallel and directly connects any two positions, unlike RNNs which process tokens sequentially and struggle to retain long-range dependencies -- parallelism made internet-scale training practical.
interview.deep_answer: RNNs process tokens one at a time, carrying a hidden state forward -- this makes training inherently sequential (can't parallelize across time steps) and causes long-range dependencies to decay (the vanishing gradient problem). Self-attention computes a direct, weighted connection between every pair of tokens in one parallel pass, both enabling much larger-scale training and giving the model a more direct path to relate distant context.

children.title: Attention
children.short_overview: The mechanism letting a model weigh how relevant each other token is when producing a representation for a given token.

sections.what: The mechanism letting a transformer weigh how relevant every other token in context is to the token currently being processed, producing a weighted blend of information from across the sequence.
sections.why: Attention is the specific innovation that lets an LLM use relevant context from anywhere in a long prompt (a retrieved document, an earlier instruction, a code file) when generating each new token -- directly explains why providing better, more relevant context improves output quality (context engineering).
sections.how: Each token is projected into Query/Key/Value vectors; attention score between two tokens is computed from the dot product of one token's Query and another's Key, scaled and passed through softmax to produce weights, which then blend the Value vectors -- 'multi-head' attention runs several of these in parallel, each potentially learning different types of relationships.
sections.when: Directly relevant to context engineering decisions: what to include/exclude/order in a prompt, since attention (and its computational cost) scales with sequence length.
sections.context: N/A -- foundational knowledge underlying model behavior; not implemented by this project, which uses attention indirectly via the Claude API.

interview.question: How does attention relate to practical prompt/context engineering?
interview.short_answer: Attention is literally the mechanism the model uses to decide which parts of your context matter for the current output -- well-structured, relevant, appropriately-ordered context gives attention better signal to work with, which is the mechanical reason context quality affects output quality.
interview.deep_answer: Since attention computes relevance dynamically per-token rather than treating all context equally, irrelevant or poorly-structured context doesn't just waste tokens -- it can dilute the attention weight available for genuinely relevant information. This is part of the real justification for this project's curated RAG corpus (a small, code-reviewed set of real files) over indexing an entire repository indiscriminately: more relevant, less noisy context.

children.title: Token
children.short_overview: The basic unit a language model reads/writes — a word, subword, or character fragment, not necessarily a whole word.

sections.what: The basic unit an LLM processes -- not always a whole word; often a sub-word piece, punctuation mark, or common multi-character sequence, determined by the model's tokenizer.
sections.why: Every cost, latency, and context-window limit an LLM API exposes is measured in tokens, not words or characters -- understanding tokens is a precondition for real cost/latency reasoning, not an academic detail.
sections.how: Text is converted to a sequence of integer token IDs via the model's tokenizer before being fed to the model; the model's output is also a sequence of token IDs, decoded back to text.
sections.when: Every time reasoning about API cost (priced per input/output token), context-window budget, or truncation behavior.
sections.context: This project's own event ledger captures real input/output token counts directly from the Anthropic API's own usage field for every genuine model call (never estimated), specifically to make token/cost reasoning accurate rather than guessed -- see AEQ-028's fix, which closed a real leak of fake token counts into that same real data.

interview.question: Why do LLM APIs price and limit by tokens instead of characters or words?
interview.short_answer: Tokens are the model's actual unit of computation -- pricing and context limits track the real cost driver (how many token-positions the model must process), which doesn't correspond 1:1 to word or character count, especially across languages or code.
interview.deep_answer: A real, concrete engineering consequence: this project's own usage/cost telemetry captures input_tokens/output_tokens directly from the API response's real usage field, using a versioned pricing table keyed by token counts -- never estimating cost from character length, which would be both inaccurate and inconsistent across different content types (code tends to tokenize differently than prose).

children.title: Tokenization
children.short_overview: Splitting raw text into tokens using a fixed vocabulary/algorithm before it can be fed to a model.

sections.what: The process of converting raw text into the model's token vocabulary -- modern LLMs typically use a sub-word algorithm (e.g. byte-pair encoding or similar), balancing vocabulary size against sequence length.
sections.why: Sub-word tokenization lets a model handle any input (including rare words, code identifiers, or misspellings) by falling back to smaller pieces, rather than failing on out-of-vocabulary whole words -- explains why code and unusual text sometimes consume more tokens than plain prose.
sections.how: A tokenizer is trained on a large corpus to find a vocabulary of common sub-word units that efficiently represents that corpus; at inference, greedy or learned merge rules split input text into the longest matching known pieces.
sections.when: Relevant when estimating real token cost for a workload (code-heavy content vs. prose tokenizes differently) or debugging unexpectedly high token usage.
sections.context: N/A -- consumed indirectly via the Anthropic API's own tokenizer; not implemented by this project.

interview.question: Why might a code snippet use more tokens than a similarly-long sentence of English prose?
interview.short_answer: Code has more unusual identifiers, symbols, and whitespace patterns than natural language, so it tends to split into more, smaller sub-word tokens relative to its character count than typical prose does.
interview.deep_answer: This has real practical implications for cost/context-budget planning in an AI coding tool: a given character-count budget for code context will typically consume more of the token-based context window than the same character count of prose, which is part of why this project's curated RAG chunks by logical code boundaries (class members, not fixed character windows) -- more semantically useful content per token spent.

children.title: Context Window
children.short_overview: The maximum number of tokens (input + output) a model can attend to in a single call.

sections.what: The maximum number of tokens (input + output combined, or sometimes tracked separately) a model can process in a single call -- everything the model 'sees' at once, with no memory beyond it unless re-supplied.
sections.why: The context window is the hard ceiling on how much information (conversation history, retrieved documents, code files) can inform a single response -- directly drives context-engineering decisions about what to include, summarize, or omit.
sections.how: Implemented via the positional encoding and attention mechanism's practical scaling limits -- larger context windows require more compute per call (attention cost scales with sequence length), so window size is both an architectural and a cost/latency trade-off.
sections.when: Every time a workload risks exceeding available context -- long conversations, large codebases, or big retrieved-document sets all need explicit context management (summarization, retrieval instead of full-inclusion, truncation strategy) once they approach the limit.
sections.context: This project's context management strategy is retrieval, not brute-force inclusion: rather than stuffing an entire repository into context, its curated RAG corpus retrieves only the top-K most relevant chunks per query, keeping context small, relevant, and within budget regardless of total corpus size.

interview.question: How do you design a system to work within a model's context window as your data grows?
interview.short_answer: Retrieval instead of brute-force inclusion -- index the full corpus once, then at query time fetch only the most relevant small subset into context, so context size stays roughly constant regardless of how large the underlying data gets.
interview.deep_answer: This project's own RAG design makes exactly this trade-off explicit: the corpus can grow (10 to 28 files, in a real disclosed change) without proportionally growing the context sent per query, because retrieval always returns a bounded top-K (5 results) regardless of corpus size -- the alternative (sending the whole corpus every time) would eventually exceed the context window and would waste tokens on irrelevant content even before hitting that hard limit.

children.title: Inference
children.short_overview: Running a trained model forward to produce an output, as opposed to training/updating its weights.

sections.what: Running a trained model to produce an output for new input -- as opposed to training, which is how the model's weights were learned in the first place. Every API call to an LLM is an inference call.
sections.why: Distinguishing inference from training matters because they have completely different cost/infrastructure profiles -- an application engineer calling an LLM API is doing inference only, with no involvement in (or cost exposure to) the original training run.
sections.how: Given input tokens, the model computes a probability distribution over its vocabulary for the next token, a token is sampled from that distribution (see sampling/temperature), appended to the sequence, and the process repeats autoregressively until a stop condition.
sections.when: Every real API call this project makes to Claude is an inference call -- relevant whenever reasoning about latency (inference time scales with output length, since tokens are generated sequentially) or cost (priced per inference call's token usage).
sections.context: Every real model call in this project (agent/reasoning_gateway.py, agent/agent_loop.py, etc.) is exactly this: pure inference against a pre-trained model, with real usage captured from each call's response.

interview.question: Why does LLM output generation feel slower for longer responses?
interview.short_answer: Inference is autoregressive -- each output token depends on all previous tokens, so tokens are generated one at a time sequentially; a longer response requires more sequential generation steps, which is why output length (not just input length) drives latency.
interview.deep_answer: This has a real, practical design consequence this project applies directly: max_tokens is set deliberately per call based on the expected real need (not maximized by default), since a larger max_tokens budget for a task that doesn't need it only risks longer latency and, in extended-thinking-capable models, risks the entire budget being consumed by reasoning before any real answer text is produced -- a real failure mode this project's reasoning_gateway.py explicitly detects and reports honestly rather than silently returning empty text.

children.title: Sampling
children.short_overview: The strategy for choosing the next token from the model's predicted probability distribution.

sections.what: The strategy for choosing the next token from the model's predicted probability distribution -- ranges from always picking the single highest-probability token (greedy/deterministic) to sampling with controlled randomness.
sections.why: Sampling strategy directly controls the trade-off between consistency/predictability and creativity/diversity in output -- a real, tunable parameter, not a fixed property of the model.
sections.how: Common strategies: greedy (always highest probability -- fully deterministic but can produce repetitive or locally-stuck output), temperature-scaled sampling (introduces controlled randomness), top-p/nucleus sampling (samples only from the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds a threshold, avoiding very-low-probability 'tail' tokens).
sections.when: Lower/no randomness for tasks needing consistency or determinism (structured data extraction, code generation where exact correctness matters); higher randomness only where creative variation is genuinely desired.
sections.context: N/A -- this project's own reasoning_gateway.py does not currently expose sampling-parameter control per call (uses API defaults), a real, honest scope boundary rather than an unused feature claimed as implemented.

interview.question: When would you turn temperature down to near-zero for an LLM call?
interview.short_answer: Whenever you need the most consistent, highest-confidence answer rather than creative variation -- structured extraction, classification-style tasks, or any case where you'll be comparing outputs across repeated runs and want them stable.
interview.deep_answer: Near-zero temperature approximates greedy decoding (always the most probable token), which is desirable when consistency matters more than diversity -- but it's worth knowing this doesn't guarantee full determinism in practice for many hosted APIs (batching, numerical non-determinism, and infrastructure-level variation can still produce different outputs for identical input), so genuine reproducibility usually still needs independent verification rather than relying on temperature=0 alone.

children.title: Temperature
children.short_overview: A sampling parameter controlling randomness — lower values make output more deterministic/focused.

sections.what: A sampling parameter that scales the model's output probability distribution before sampling -- lower values sharpen the distribution toward the most likely tokens (more deterministic), higher values flatten it (more random/diverse).
sections.why: The single most commonly discussed LLM API tuning knob -- understanding what it actually does (rescaling a probability distribution, not 'creativity' as a vague concept) lets an engineer reason about it precisely rather than treating it as a magic dial.
sections.how: Before sampling, each token's logit (raw score) is divided by the temperature value; dividing by a value less than 1 sharpens the distribution (temperature -> 0 approaches greedy/argmax), dividing by a value greater than 1 flattens it toward uniform.
sections.when: Low temperature for tasks needing consistency/correctness; higher temperature only for tasks genuinely wanting varied, creative output across repeated calls.
sections.context: N/A -- not currently tuned per-call by this project (API default used); honest scope, not a hidden gap.

interview.question: Explain temperature to someone who's never heard the term.
interview.short_answer: It's a knob that controls how 'confident vs. exploratory' the model's next-word choice is -- low temperature almost always picks the single most likely next token, high temperature gives less-likely tokens a real chance of being picked too.
